title: Self-taught solo style with nobody to copy in 1918
summary: Lee, Driver and Waters played original solos because they had heard no Bechet or Armstrong; improvising just means knowing the chords, and New York later changed his sound.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Yeah. So we have you - well, wait a second, you made the comment yesterday when we were talking about blues singer over at the radio station -

That somebody could be in a school. Would you say the solos of Driver, Lee and yourself in the Charlie Miller Jazz Orchestra, we're speaking of the 'teens now, late 'teens in Philadelphia, were of the same school or more primitive in nature in what a jazz solo was to the innovations of Bechet and Armstrong that we hear on records a few years later?

Well, I would say it was a little bit different, see. But Bill, Bill Lee could play a much, very much trumpet, a lot of trumpet, and he improvised real well in correct harmonies. But it didn't sound like Louis Armstrong. And I could play a lot of saxophone and improvise, but I wasn't copying Sidney Bechet because I didn't hear much of, that much of those, that period, you see what i mean? So that's what I'm saying, that [ ] -
Well, there's no way you could have been copying these people in 1918 because you didn't even know they existed.
Yeah, that's what I've been saying, see so -

The question I'm asking you to do try to do is - if possible - is that you've got, you're taking solos, Bill Lee is takin' solos, Driver is takin' solos, it's 1918 and nobody's heard of Sidney Bechet, nobody's heard of Louis Armstrong in the Haverford, Philadelphia -

Pennsylvania area. Is the music that you people were playing as solos of the nature, of the school that we become more familiar with through records a few years later - I mean, when I say "we" I mean me, and -

Yeah, sure, well you see, because it's just like - you see, improvising, you don't play like Louis Armstrong or Sidney Bechet to sound good, you see what I mean? Because you can sound good without - I could even say that Bill had a kind of original style and so did I, particularly at that period on the alto saxophone. I sound more like somebody now because I came to New York and was associated with Benny Carter, worked with Benny Carter, worked with Earl Bostic, worked with Johnny Hodg[es] - listened to all these other cats, Frankie Trumbauer and all these guys like that, listen - then you got that when you listen like that in New York, it's a mecca for jazz, more so than New Orleans, you know. 'Cause it has more of a variety, you know - more of a variety of playing -

And you adopt, get adapted to some of those sounds that you hear, automatically without even rehearsing or practicing or trying things out. But then, there, it was nobody to listen to, you had to play with your - so anybody can play, improvise if they know the harmony. See, you don't have to have no guide, you just play the harmony. If a chord is a C seven and you just practicin', use a C seven in different ways. And it may not sound like that person or that person but it will be correct, see what I mean?
